content.text:
**Letter B**, on both counts.

**Clarity — B.** B tells the clients up front exactly what is being reported on (the three accounts, run to one model), so the numbers have a stated scope; A never says what "the account" refers to. B also glosses the terms rather than just using them — "net of fees, that is, after the advisory fees you actually paid" — which is precisely what a non-specialist needs to read the performance block without guessing. The section headings and the one-idea-per-block structure let a reader find the fee change or the trades without re-reading. A runs performance, positioning, and a fee change through undifferentiated paragraphs, and its comparison sentence — "outperformed the index, which declined by -3.2%" — makes the reader untangle a double negative to work out who did better. A's fee paragraph also buries the mechanics (effective date, first invoice, billing basis) in a single long closing sentence, where B sets out the old rate, new rate, unchanged tier, and timing in sequence.

**Tone — B.** The notes call for precise and unhurried with no superlatives, for two analytical readers. A opens the positioning section with "navigating a challenging global environment while maintaining our long-term objectives," which is filler that says nothing and will read as padding to clients who go through attribution line by line. "We are pleased to inform you" and "As this is a benefit to you" editorialize a fee cut that speaks for itself, and "took advantage of market volatility" claims more skill than the facts assert. B states the trades flatly and lets the reduction stand on its own merits, then closes with an offer to walk through the attribution in detail — exactly the register these two clients are described as wanting. B's only mild lapses are "put back to work" and the bolding, neither of which strikes a promotional note.

**Overall — B.** It is the letter I would send. A is competent but generic; B is written for these particular readers.

input.reason: Clarity: B states the reporting scope (three named accounts run to one model) so the figures have context, glosses net vs. gross in plain language, and uses section headings with one idea per block so the fee change and portfolio changes are findable. A never identifies what "the account" covers, forces the reader through a double negative ("outperformed the index, which declined by -3.2%"), and compresses the fee mechanics into one long closing sentence. Tone: the notes ask for precise, unhurried, no superlatives for two analytical readers. A adds empty framing ("navigating a challenging global environment while maintaining our long-term objectives"), self-congratulation ("we are pleased to inform you," "as this is a benefit to you"), and an unsupported skill claim ("took advantage of market volatility"). B reports the trades flatly, lets the fee reduction stand on its own, and closes by offering to walk through the attribution, which matches clients described as reading attribution line by line. B's only minor blemishes are the mild idiom "put back to work" and the bolding, which aids scanning more than it markets. Overall B on both dimensions; length was not a factor.
